relations.note: Adam fathers Cain, though no conversation or further action between them is recorded.
Enoch is Adam’s seventh-generation descendant; Genesis narrates no meeting.
Adam transmits the principle of calendar intercalation to Enoch.
Eve is Adam’s corresponding partner, wife, and mother of his children.
Eve gives Adam fruit from the prohibited tree, and he eats.
Eve gives Adam the forbidden fruit; together they are judged and expelled.
Nimrod possesses the divinely made garments originally belonging to Adam.
Cain fathers Enoch and names a city after him.
Eve conceives, bears, and names Cain with a qnh wordplay.
Job and Daniel or Danel appear jointly in Ezekiel’s righteous triad.
Josephus portrays Delilah as Samson's prostitute and cohabiting lover among the Philistines.
Pseudo-Philo makes Delilah a Philistine harlot whom Samson takes as his wife.
Rabbinic elaboration identifies Delilah as Samson's wife and emphasizes her sexual coercion.
Milton makes Dalila Samson's wife; she defends her betrayal, but he rejects her.
DeMille reinvents Delilah as Samson's romantic partner within an elaborate prior relationship.

relations.myth: The four tests of Samson's strength
relations.note: Delilah extracts Samson's secret, arranges his shaving, and enables his capture.
The opera expands Delilah's betrayal into a religious and political conspiracy.
DeMille dramatizes Delilah's betrayal, subsequent repentance, and presence at Samson's death.
Samson loves Delilah, although Judges never states that she reciprocates.
The opera portrays Dalila using feigned desire to secure Samson's secret for Philistia.
Some Christian apocalypses pair Elijah and Enoch against Antichrist.
Later Christian tradition pairs Enoch and Elijah as deathless end-time witnesses.
Elijah awakens Jacob separately to pray for redemption.
Nimrod possesses garments originally made by God for Adam and Eve.
Samson and Gideon appear together in a catalogue of figures empowered through faith.
Job becomes Jacob’s son-in-law when later tradition identifies his wife as Dinah.

relations.myth: Jacob gives Joseph the distinctive robe
relations.note: Jacob favors Joseph and gives him the robe that provokes his brothers' jealousy.
Joseph is Jacob's favored son by Rachel.
Joseph sends his shirt, which restores his father's sight before their reunion.
Under the Amraphel equation, Nimrod's coalition captures Lot.

god_relations.note: Michael leads angelic service at Adam’s death, burial, and promised restoration.
Some Latter-day Saint teachings identify Adam with the archangel Michael.
Gabriel participates in Adam’s funeral or heavenly service in some later recensions.
god_relations.source: Life of Adam and Eve tradition

god_relations.note: Raphael appears among named angels in portions of Adam literature; his role varies.
Medieval tradition makes Lilith Adam’s first wife before Eve.
Adam demands precedence; Lilith asserts equality, invokes the divine name, and leaves.
Wisdom protects and delivers the first-formed father after his transgression.
The Gnostic chief ruler fathers Cain through sexual violation of Eve.

god_relations.myth: Yaldabaoth deceptively names his archontic offspring
god_relations.note: Yaldabaoth deceptively gives one of his generated rulers the name Cain.
Later Gnostic and Jewish legends make the serpent-Samael Cain’s supernatural father.

god_relations.myth: Sophia rescues Cain’s higher spiritual element
god_relations.note: Reported Gnostic systems say Sophia rescues Cain’s higher element from the creator’s assault.

god_relations.myth: Interpretation of the ram and goat
god_relations.note: Gabriel explains Daniel’s vision of Media, Persia, Greece, and Antiochus.
Gabriel explains the seventy-week timetable following Daniel’s prayer.
Michael protects Daniel’s people and assists the messenger bringing Daniel revelation.
Daniel refuses worship, exposes the priests’ fraud, and destroys Bel’s image and temple.
Raphael shows Enoch places of punishment.
Michael guides Enoch and explains heavenly mysteries and judgment.
Michael clothes or anoints Enoch before God in some recensions.

god_relations.myth: Holy angels report the Watcher crisis
god_relations.note: Gabriel appears among the holy angels during judgment of the Watchers and giants.
Gabriel brings books or revelation to Idrīs-Enoch in later Islamic legend.
Enoch reports or witnesses Asael's punishment for teaching forbidden arts.
The exalted Enoch explicitly becomes the angel Metatron.
Modern theories linked Esther’s name and role with Ishtar, without ancient textual identification.
Michael and other angels assist Eve during her agonizing childbirth.
Samael animates or rides the serpent and engineers Eve’s temptation.
Gideon cuts down Asherah’s cult object and burns its wood in sacrifice.
Michael is sent to Jacob shortly before the patriarch's death.
Later tradition identifies Samael as Jacob's opponent at the Jabbok.
Behemoth is shown as a mighty creature beyond Job’s mastery.
Job is challenged to capture or domesticate Leviathan but never encounters it.

god_relations.myth: Gabriel brings guidance or relief to Ayyūb
god_relations.note: Some later Islamic narratives make Gabriel the bearer of divine guidance or relief.

god_relations.myth: Jonah frightens Leviathan beneath the cosmic sea
god_relations.note: Jonah displays Abraham’s covenantal seal, drives Leviathan away, and vows its future capture.

god_relations.myth: Gabriel directs Joseph toward his brothers
god_relations.note: Later interpretation identifies Joseph's unnamed guide near Shechem as the angel Gabriel.
Later interpreters identify Michael as the unnamed commander encountered by Joshua.
Lot's wife sees the descending Shekhinah and becomes salt.
Michael descends to rescue Abraham from the furnace ordered by Nimrod.
Gabriel assists or addresses Abraham during Nimrod's furnace episode.
Modern scholars propose Ninurta as Nimrod's etymological or typological divine model.
Hislop-derived literature claims Tammuz was Nimrod's posthumous or reincarnated son.
Modern comparison links their lion-slaying, exceptional strength, erotic vulnerability, and violent deaths without establishing identity.
Modern structural comparison invokes prodigious strength and women's roles, without ancient interaction or demonstrated transmission.
Modern scholarship makes broad structural comparisons, but documents no ancient interaction or identification.
Solomon follows or accommodates the Ammonite deity Milcom.
Solomon builds a high place for the Moabite deity Chemosh.
The Solomonic speaker desires personified Wisdom as his companion through prayer.
Michael gives Solomon a ring bearing a divine seal.
Solomon binds, interrogates, and assigns Asmodeus labor on the Temple.

Abezithibod.note: Solomon imprisons the Red Sea demon with Ephippas's assistance.

Abraham.note: Elijah awakens Abraham separately to pray for redemption.
The Septuagint genealogy makes Job fifth in descent from Abraham through Esau.
Lot accompanies Abram and Sarai from Haran into Canaan.
Abram defeats Lot's captors and recovers him, his goods and household.
Rabbinic tradition says Lot learned hospitality from Abraham.
Lūṭ accepts Ibrāhīm's message and declares his migration to God.

Abraham.myth: Debate over God and the elements
Abraham.note: Nimrod debates Abraham about which element or power deserves worship.
Nimrod orders Abraham burned, but God preserves Abraham in the fire.

Abraham.myth: Debate over life, death, and sun
Abraham.note: Nimrod is identified as the unnamed ruler whom Abraham defeats in argument.
Under the Amraphel equation, Nimrod's coalition is defeated by Abraham.

Allah.note: Guides and elects Yaʿqūb as a prophet and righteous ancestor.
Allah removes Ayyūb’s distress, provides healing water, and restores his family.
Allah praises Ayyūb as patient and an excellent servant.

Anafiel.note: Anafiel is associated with Enoch-Metatron's admission or guidance in heavenly palaces.

Ancient of Days.note: Daniel sees the Ancient of Days enthroned and judging the beastly kingdoms.

Angel of YHWH.myth: The song quotes the angel’s curse against Meroz
Angel of YHWH.note: Deborah’s song voice reports the angel’s curse upon Meroz for withholding aid.

Angel of Yahweh.note: The messenger announces Samson's birth and consecration to his parents before he is born.

Angel of the Sun.note: The Angel of the Sun helps Idrīs-Enoch ascend in Islamic legend.

Angel/messenger of God.note: Reveals that God transferred Laban's livestock increase to Jacob.
Orders Jacob to leave Laban and return to his homeland.
Hosea identifies Jacob's divine opponent as an angel or messenger.

Angels of God.myth: Angels ascend and descend at Bethel
Angels of God.note: Jacob sees divine messengers moving between earth and heaven.
Divine messengers encounter Jacob during his return journey.

Araqiel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Araqiel among the descended Watchers.

Ark/Zion.note: Personified Zion leaves Solomon's Jerusalem for Ethiopia, transferring divine election.

Armaros.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Armaros among the descended Watchers.

Asenath.note: Asenath is Joseph's Egyptian wife and the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim.

Asenath.myth: Asenath converts and becomes Joseph's heavenly bride
Asenath.note: The romance expands their marriage into Asenath's conversion and a conspiracy against the couple.

Asher.note: Asher is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual encounter is narrated.

Ashmedai.note: Solomon has Ashmedai captured through Benaiah to learn the shamir's location.
Ashmedai tricks Solomon, steals his ring, hurls him away, and supplants him.

Ashtoreth.note: Solomon goes after the Sidonian goddess under his foreign wives' influence.

Asshur.note: Ambiguous syntax makes either Nimrod or Asshur the founder departing Shinar for Assyria.

Awan.note: Jubilees names Awan as Adam and Eve’s daughter and Cain’s wife.
Jubilees identifies Awan as Cain’s sister.
Cain marries his sister Awan in Jubilees.
Jubilees names Awan as Eve’s daughter.

Ayyūb’s wife.note: Post-Qurʾānic narratives commonly name Ayyūb’s faithful wife Raḥma.

Ayyūb’s wife.myth: Ayyūb fulfills his oath with a bundle
Ayyūb’s wife.note: Later exegesis says Ayyūb symbolically strikes his wife without violating his oath.

Azura.note: Jubilees names Azura as Adam and Eve’s daughter and Seth’s wife.
Jubilees names Azura as Eve’s daughter.

Baal.note: Elijah challenges Baal’s prophets and mocks Baal’s failure to answer.
Ilyās condemns his people for invoking Baʿl instead of God.
Gideon destroys Baal’s altar, prompting the polemical name Jerubbaal.

Baal-zebub of Ekron.note: Elijah condemns Ahaziah’s consultation of Baal-zebub, without encountering the god.

Balaam.note: Rabbinic legend makes Job and Balaam fellow advisers in Pharaoh’s court.

Barak.note: Samson and Barak appear together in a catalogue of figures empowered through faith.

Baraka.note: Jubilees names Baraka as Enoch's mother.

Baraqel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Baraqel among the descended Watchers.

Bedan.note: Rabbinic interpretation identifies Samson with Bedan through the wordplay ben Dan.

Beelzeboul.note: Solomon compels the demon prince to command demons and assist construction.

Ben-ammi.note: Ben-ammi is Lot's son and grandson through the younger daughter.

Benjamin.note: Benjamin is Joseph's full brother, sharing both Jacob and Rachel as parents.

Benjamin.myth: Joseph plants the cup in Benjamin's sack
Benjamin.note: Joseph secretly plants his cup and detains Benjamin to test their brothers.

Beriah.note: Beriah is listed among Joseph's descendants through Ephraim.

Bildad the Shuhite.note: Bildad debates Job, defends traditional retribution, and implicates Job’s dead children.

Bildad the Shuhite.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
Bildad the Shuhite.note: Job’s prayer accompanies Bildad’s required closing sacrifice.

Christ.note: Paul opposes Adam’s disobedience and death to Christ’s obedience and life.
Later Christian tradition depicts Christ liberating Adam from Hades.
Patristic exegesis treats Job as a type of Christ rather than a companion.

Commander of YHWH’s army.note: The armed figure confronts Joshua and orders him to remove his sandal.

Cupid.note: Rubens adds Cupid as classical interpretive imagery within the scene of Delilah's betrayal.

Cush.note: Cush is named as Nimrod's father or immediate ancestor.
Cush gives Nimrod the garments originally made for Adam and Eve.

Dagon.note: Samson destroys Dagon's temple and worshippers, enacting the narrative's Yahweh–Dagon rivalry.

Dan.note: Dan is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual interaction is narrated.

David.note: Samson and David appear together in a catalogue of figures empowered through faith.

Dinah.note: Several later Jewish traditions make Jacob’s daughter Dinah Job’s wife.
Dinah.source: Pseudo-Philo; Testament of Job; Genesis Rabbah

Edni/Edna.note: Jubilees names Edni or Edna as Enoch's wife.

Eliezer of Damascus.note: A late variant makes Eliezer Nimrod's son.

Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite.myth: Elihu rebukes Job and the friends
Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite.note: Elihu attacks Job’s claims and argues that suffering can discipline or instruct.

Eliphaz the Temanite.note: Eliphaz consoles, accuses, and debates Job about suffering and divine justice.

Eliphaz the Temanite.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
Eliphaz the Temanite.note: Job prays for Eliphaz after YHWH orders sacrifice and intercession.

Elisha.note: Elisha accepts Elijah’s mantle-call and becomes his attendant and successor.
Elijah leaves Elisha his mantle and an heir’s portion of spirit.
Medieval Islamic narratives restore the biblical master-successor relationship.

Eloim.note: A Gnostic recension identifies or pairs Cain with the archontic ruler Eloim.

Enepsigos.note: The triple-shaped lunar demon predicts future events and Solomon's downfall.

Enoch the visionary.myth: Enoch witnesses Abel’s accusation against Cain
Enoch the visionary.note: Enoch encounters Abel’s spirit continuing its accusation until Cain’s lineage is destroyed.

Enoch the visionary.myth: Enoch sees Cain as a dark bovine
Enoch the visionary.note: Enoch’s animal vision represents Cain as a dark bovine killing red Abel.

Enosh.note: Enosh is a named ancestor of Enoch.

Ephippas.note: Solomon captures Ephippas and makes the wind-demon lift a cornerstone.
Ephippas helps Solomon capture and imprison Abezithibod.

Ephraim.note: Ephraim is Joseph's second son by Asenath.

Esau.note: Irenaeus reports Cain and Esau grouped as spiritual kin opposing the creator.
The Septuagint appendix places Job within Esau’s Edomite lineage.
Esau kills Nimrod and takes the garments originally made for Adam.

Ezeqeel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Ezeqeel among the descended Watchers.

Gad.note: Gad is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual encounter is narrated.

Gadreel.note: The fallen angel Gadreel is credited with leading Eve astray.

God.note: God creates Adam or humanity from earth, clay, or dust.
God questions Adam, sentences him to toil and mortality, and expels him.
God teaches Adam all the names, whose knowledge Adam demonstrates to the angels.
Luke places Adam at the genealogy’s end as son of God.
God appoints Lūṭ as prophet and messenger to his people.
God saves Lūṭ and his household except his unbelieving wife.

God / YHWH.myth: Enoch walks with God and is taken
God / YHWH.note: Enoch walks with God before God mysteriously takes him.
God transforms Enoch, granting wings, glory, a throne, and celestial authority.

God of Israel.myth: Daniel receives wisdom and knowledge of dreams
God of Israel.note: God grants Daniel exceptional wisdom, knowledge, and insight into dreams.

God of Israel.myth: Daniel prays despite the royal prohibition
God of Israel.note: Daniel faithfully prays to God despite the decree that leads to the lions’ pit.
God sends an angel who shuts the lions’ mouths and preserves Daniel.

God of Israel.myth: Promise to stand at the end
God of Israel.note: God’s revelation promises Daniel an allotted portion at the resurrection.

God of Israel.myth: Esther’s unsummoned approach to the king
God of Israel.note: God answers Esther’s prayer and changes the king’s spirit to gentleness.

God of Israel.myth: Judith prays, credits God, and leads the victory hymn
God of Israel.note: Judith seeks divine aid, attributes her victory to God, and leads Israel’s praise.
Judith dedicates Holofernes’s canopy and gives the captured spoils to God.

Hahyah.note: Hahyah seeks Enoch's interpretation of dreams foretelling the giants' destruction.

Ham.note: Nimrod is Ham's grandson through Cush.
Ham removes Adam's garments from the ark and transmits them through Cush to Nimrod.

Haran.note: Nimrod casts Haran into the furnace after Abraham, and Haran dies.

Hermes Trismegistus.note: Islamicate learned tradition identifies Enoch-Idrīs with the first Hermes.

Iblīs.note: Iblīs tempts Adam and his spouse, causing their lapse and descent.
Iblīs refuses to prostrate to Adam, claiming fiery superiority over clay.
Iblīs whispers to Adam and his spouse and causes their expulsion.
Later Islamic stories make Iblīs personally cause Ayyūb’s losses and disease.

Ibrāhīm/Abraham.note: Joseph descends from Abraham and professes adherence to his ancestral religion.

Idrīs.note: Idrīs and Ilyās belong to a reported scheme of four living prophets.
Post-Qurʾānic Islamic exegesis identifies Enoch with the prophet Idrīs.

Irad.note: Cain is Irad’s genealogical ancestor through Enoch.

Isaac.note: Elijah awakens Isaac separately to pray for redemption.

Issachar.note: Issachar is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual encounter is narrated.

Isḥāq/Isaac.note: Joseph is Isaac's grandson and names him among the ancestral prophets he follows.

Jabal.note: Cain is Jabal’s genealogical ancestor through Lamech and Adah.

Jemimah.note: Jemimah is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.

Jephthah.note: Samson and Jephthah appear together in a catalogue of figures empowered through faith.

Jesus.note: Elijah appears with Moses and speaks with the transfigured Jesus.
Jesus and Ilyās belong to a reported scheme of four living prophets.
Christian interpretation places Jacob's ascending and descending angels upon Jesus.
Jesus invokes Jonah as a sign, connecting his ordeal with resurrection and Nineveh’s repentance.
Jesus invokes Solomon's wisdom and glory but declares something greater present.

Jesus Christ.myth: Cain’s hatred contrasts with Christlike self-giving love
Jesus Christ.note: Cain’s evil murder is contrasted with the self-giving love exemplified by Christ.
Enoch preaches faith in Christ and sees his future coming.
Christian interpreters read Gideon’s fleece, jars, torches, and victory as figures of Christ.
Christian exegesis typologically parallels Joseph's betrayal, suffering, salvation, and exaltation with Christ.
Christian writers typologically equate Joshua with Jesus through their shared Greek name and succession symbolism.
Jesus Christ.source: Barnabas 12; Justin; Origen, Homilies on Joshua

Jesus Christ.note: Christian exegetes interpret Samson as a type of Christ, especially through betrayal and victorious death.

Jethro.note: Jethro opposes Pharaoh and flees, contrasting with Job’s alleged silence.

Jobab.myth: Greek appendix identifies Job as Jobab
Jobab.note: The Septuagint appendix equates Job with the Edomite king Jobab.

Job’s three daughters.myth: Job gives his daughters heavenly cords
Job’s three daughters.note: Job gives them supernatural cords enabling angelic speech and celestial hymnody.

Job’s unnamed wife.note: The Hebrew book presents an unnamed woman as Job’s wife.

Job’s unnamed wife.myth: Job’s wife urges him to curse God
Job’s unnamed wife.note: She urges Job to bless or curse God and die; Job rebukes her.

John the Baptist.note: John functionally fulfills Elijah’s expected return in spirit and power.
John denies that he is literally Elijah, creating a canonical variant.

Jubal.note: Cain is Jubal’s genealogical ancestor through Lamech and Adah.

Judah.note: Judah persuades the brothers to sell Joseph rather than kill him.

Judah.myth: Judah offers himself and Joseph reveals his identity
Judah.note: Judah's plea to replace Benjamin moves Joseph to reveal himself to his brothers.

Judas Iscariot.myth: Cainite heresiology groups Cain with Judas
Judas Iscariot.note: Heresiologists associate reverence for Cain with a positive valuation of Judas.

Kenan.note: Kenan is a named ancestor of Enoch.

Keren-happuch.note: Keren-happuch is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.

Keziah.note: Keziah is Job’s restored daughter and receives an inheritance.

Kokabel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Kokabel among the descended Watchers.

Korah.note: Irenaeus reports Cain and Korah grouped among figures opposing the creator.

Lamech.note: Cain is Lamech’s ancestor in the Cainite genealogy.
Lamech magnifies Cain’s sevenfold vengeance into a seventy-sevenfold boast.
Later legend identifies Cain as the victim accidentally shot by blind Lamech.

Levi.note: Levi is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual encounter is narrated.

Lot's wife.note: She is Lot's unnamed wife in Genesis and the Qurʾan.
Islamic tradition says she betrays Lūṭ by disclosing his angelic guests.

Machir.note: Machir is Joseph's grandson through Manasseh.

Mahalalel.note: Mahalalel is a named ancestor of Enoch.

Mahaway.note: Mahaway travels to Enoch seeking interpretation of the giants' ominous dreams.

Mahijah/Mahujah.note: Mahijah or Mahujah questions Enoch and prompts his prophetic preaching.

Manasseh.note: Manasseh is Joseph's first son by Asenath.

Mary.note: Christian interpreters treated Esther’s royal intercession as a type of Mary’s heavenly intercession.
Mary’s obedience typologically reverses Eve’s disobedience; they never meet.

Mehujael.note: Cain is Mehujael’s ancestor in the Cainite genealogy.

Messenger/Angel of YHWH.note: The messenger calls Gideon, consumes his offering with fire, and disappears.

Messiah.note: Elijah heralds, attends, and conveys information about the coming Messiah.

Methuselah.note: Enoch fathers Methuselah at age sixty-five.
Enoch gives Methuselah revealed books and instruction.
Enoch gives Methuselah ethical, liturgical, and priestly instruction.

Methushael.note: Cain is Methushael’s ancestor in the Cainite genealogy.

Moab.note: Moab is Lot's son and grandson through the elder daughter.

Molech.note: Masoretic wording attributes a shrine for Molech to Solomon.

Moses.note: Elijah and Moses appear together and speak with Jesus.

Moses.myth: Job placed in the time of Moses
Moses.note: One rabbinic strand makes Job Moses’ contemporary and says Moses wrote his book.

Moses.myth: Moses carries Joseph's bones from Egypt
Moses.note: Moses fulfills Joseph's oath by carrying his remains during the Exodus.

Muḥammad.note: During the miʿrāj, Muḥammad meets Adam in the first heaven.

Naamah.note: Cain is Naamah’s genealogical ancestor through Lamech and Zillah.

Naphtali.note: Naphtali is Joseph's paternal half-brother; Genesis narrates no individual interaction.

Noah.note: Noah descends from Adam, although no canonical meeting is narrated.
Enoch's warnings and records are transmitted through his family toward Noah.
Job and Noah appear together as proverbial righteous men without meeting.
Lot's wife and Noah's wife are paired as unbelievers married to righteous servants.
Nimrod is Noah's great-grandson through Ham and Cush.
The later garment-chain passes through Noah's ark before eventually reaching Nimrod.

Obyzouth.note: Solomon binds and publicly displays the infant-strangling female demon.

Ohyah.note: Ohyah seeks Enoch's interpretation of dreams foretelling the giants' destruction.

One like a son of man.note: Daniel sees this humanlike heavenly figure receive everlasting dominion.

Ornias.note: Solomon binds the child-attacking demon with the divine-seal ring.
The bound Ornias is forced to summon Beelzeboul before Solomon.

Perun.note: Slavic Christianity transfers selected thunder, rain, and fiery-vehicle functions from Perun to Elijah.

Phanuel.note: Enoch sees Phanuel attending the Chosen One as angel of repentance and hope.

Phinehas.note: Late midrash identifies Elijah with Phinehas because both display covenantal zeal.

Potiphar.note: Potiphar purchases Joseph and appoints him steward over his household.

Potiphar.myth: Potiphar imprisons Joseph after the accusation
Potiphar.note: Potiphar has Joseph imprisoned after hearing his wife's allegation.

Potiphar’s wife.note: She repeatedly demands sex from Joseph, who refuses and flees.

Potiphar’s wife.myth: The rejected wife falsely accuses Joseph
Potiphar’s wife.note: She uses Joseph's abandoned garment to accuse him of attempted sexual assault.

Pravuil/Vreveil.note: The archangel instructs Enoch and assists his production of hundreds of books.

Prince of Persia.note: This celestial adversary delays the messenger carrying an answer to Daniel.

Rachel.note: Rachel is Joseph's mother; she dies before his adult story begins.

Raguel.note: Raguel shows Enoch cosmic regions and vengeance upon errant luminaries.

Reuben.myth: Reuben attempts to save Joseph from murder
Reuben.note: Reuben redirects the brothers toward the pit, intending to return Joseph safely to Jacob.

Saint George.note: Levantine traditions make Saint George cultically interchangeable with Elijah and al-Khiḍr.

Samuel.note: Samson and Samuel appear together in a catalogue of figures empowered through faith.

Sarah.note: Sarah travels with Abram and Lot from Haran into Canaan.

Saraqiel/Sariel.note: Saraqiel or Sariel appears among holy angels associated with spirits or human sin.

Sariel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Sariel among the descended Watchers.

Satan.note: Satan deceives the first couple and later obstructs their penitence.
Satan says he fell after refusing Michael’s command to honor God’s image in Adam.
Some later legendary forms make Satan Cain’s father through Eve.

Satan.myth: Satan instructs Cain how to murder
Satan.note: Islamic tales sometimes have Satan demonstrate or instruct Cain in killing Abel.
Enoch sees Satan holding a great chain over the earth.
Satan uses the serpent to bring about Eve’s deception.
Disguised as an angel, Satan persuades Eve to abandon her penance early.
Satan.source: Latin Life of Adam and Eve

Satan.note: Job destroys Satan’s idol, and Satan retaliates through disguises and disasters.

Satan/Lucifer.note: Patristic typology and modern prophecy portray Nimrod as Satanic or Antichrist-like.

Semiramis.note: Hislopian systems claim Semiramis was Nimrod's wife; ancient evidence does not support it.
Some Hislop-derived accounts additionally claim Semiramis was Nimrod's mother.

Seth.note: Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness at the age of 130.
Adam transmits final traditions or counter-Genesis revelation to Seth.
Seth.source: Life of Adam and Eve; Apocalypse of Adam

Seth.myth: Seth replaces the Abel whom Cain killed
Seth.note: Seth is appointed as replacement seed for Abel, Cain’s murdered brother.
Seth is a named ancestor of Enoch.
Eve bears and names Seth as replacement seed for Abel.

Shamsiel.note: Enoch's collective judgment addresses Shamsiel among the descended Watchers.

Shem.note: Shem, often identified with Melchizedek, transports Adam’s body to Golgotha.
Modern Hislop-derived retellings allege that Shem executed and dismembered Nimrod.

Shemihazah.note: Enoch carries Shemihazah's petition and announces condemnation of the Watchers.

Shuthelah.note: Shuthelah is listed among Joseph's descendants through Ephraim.

Simeon.myth: Joseph binds Simeon as a hostage
Simeon.note: Joseph imprisons Simeon until the brothers return to Egypt with Benjamin.

Sitis/Sitidos.note: The Testament names Sitis or Sitidos as Job’s first wife.

Sitis/Sitidos.myth: Sitis sustains Job during Satan’s attack
Sitis/Sitidos.note: Sitis supports Job, sells her hair for bread, and dies after lamenting.

Terah.note: Lot is Terah's grandson through Haran.
Terah leads Lot and the ancestral household from Ur to Haran.
Expanded legends make Terah a court servant who delivers Abraham to Nimrod.

The Chosen One / Son of Man.note: Enoch beholds the preexistent eschatological judge concealed with God.
Chapter 71 may identify Enoch with the Son of Man, though interpretation remains disputed.

The Head of Days.note: Enoch sees the enthroned Head of Days with the Chosen One.

The dragon.note: Daniel refuses to worship the cult animal and kills it with a prepared mixture.

Tubal-Cain.note: Cain is Tubal-Cain’s genealogical ancestor through Lamech and Zillah.
Later legend makes Tubal-Cain direct blind Lamech when Lamech accidentally kills Cain.

Unnamed angel of YHWH.note: The angel twice supplies food and water to the despairing prophet.
The angel authorizes Elijah to descend safely with the third captain.

Unnamed man.note: Wrestles Jacob until dawn and wounds his hip.
Blesses Jacob and gives him the name Israel.

Uriel.note: Uriel appears among named angels in portions of Adam literature; his role varies.

Uriel.myth: Revelation of luminaries and cosmic places
Uriel.note: Uriel guides Enoch and explains celestial regions, history, and luminaries.
Uriel opposes Jacob's exalted heavenly counterpart in the fragmentary account.
Uriel reminds Jacob that Israel is his primordial angelic name.

Venus.note: Rubens adds Venus as classical interpretive imagery within the scene of Delilah's betrayal.

YHWH.myth: Cain presents produce as an offering
YHWH.note: Cain offers fruit of the ground, but YHWH does not regard it.

YHWH.myth: YHWH warns Cain about crouching sin
YHWH.note: YHWH warns the angry Cain that sin desires him and must be mastered.

YHWH.myth: YHWH interrogates Cain after Abel’s murder
YHWH.note: YHWH questions Cain and exposes Abel’s blood crying from the ground.
YHWH curses Cain from the soil and condemns him to wandering.

YHWH.myth: YHWH grants Cain a protective sign
YHWH.note: YHWH protects Cain from retaliatory killing with a sign and sevenfold vengeance.

YHWH.myth: Deborah commands Barak and sings YHWH’s victory
YHWH.note: Deborah transmits YHWH’s command, announces his aid, and praises his victory.

YHWH.myth: Jael fulfills the divinely foretold defeat of Sisera
YHWH.note: YHWH’s victory plan is indirectly fulfilled when Jael kills Sisera.
Elijah obeys YHWH’s commands and champions his exclusive worship.
YHWH answers Elijah with fire and subsequently restores rain.
YHWH corrects Elijah’s isolation claim and commissions further succession.

YHWH.myth: Gideon’s call and war against Midian
YHWH.note: YHWH commissions Gideon, reassures him, reduces his army, and grants victory.
YHWH grants Gideon two miraculous fleece signs confirming his promised deliverance.
Appears to Jacob, promises land, descendants, protection, and return.
Renames Jacob Israel and renews ancestral promises.
Hosea recalls Jacob struggling with God and seeking a blessing.

YHWH.myth: The heavenly court and Job’s testing
YHWH.note: YHWH praises Job and permits the accuser to test him under limits.

YHWH.myth: YHWH answers Job from the whirlwind
YHWH.note: YHWH confronts Job with creation’s vastness without explaining his suffering.

YHWH.myth: Job’s fortunes and family are restored
YHWH.note: YHWH accepts Job’s intercession and restores his prosperity and family.

YHWH.myth: Jonah’s two commissions to preach against Nineveh
YHWH.note: YHWH twice commissions Jonah, who eventually delivers the warning to Nineveh.

YHWH.myth: Storm and confinement following Jonah’s flight
YHWH.note: YHWH sends the storm and appoints the fish after Jonah flees.
YHWH hears Jonah’s prayer and commands the fish to expel him.

YHWH.myth: Plant, worm, wind, and lesson about Nineveh
YHWH.note: YHWH uses appointed creatures and weather to challenge Jonah’s lack of pity.
Joshua obeys YHWH’s commands and leads Israel under divine authority.
YHWH promises Joshua divine presence and gives Israel the land.
YHWH spares Lot because he remembers Abraham.
YHWH appears to Solomon and grants wisdom, riches, and honor.
YHWH promises to divide Solomon's kingdom because he follows foreign gods.
God grants Solomon prophecy, command of wind, and authority over jinn.

YHWH / God.note: Nimrod is called a mighty hunter before YHWH; no direct speech occurs.
God destroys Nimrod through an army of gnats or one brain-tormenting gnat.

YHWH God.note: God builds Eve from the human’s side as his corresponding partner.
God questions Eve and pronounces an oracle concerning pregnancy, desire, and rule.
God clothes Eve and Adam, then expels them from Eden.

YHWH/God.myth: Joseph prospers and preserves life through divine providence
YHWH/God.note: God grants Joseph favor, dream interpretation, authority, and the means to preserve life.

Yahweh.note: Yahweh chooses Samson before birth, blesses him, and appoints him to begin Israel's deliverance.
Yahweh's spirit repeatedly grants Samson extraordinary strength against the Philistines.
Yahweh answers Samson's plea by opening a hollow and providing water.
Yahweh departs after Samson's consecrated hair is shaved, leaving him powerless.
Yahweh answers Samson's final prayer by restoring strength for the fatal collapse.

Zare.note: The Septuagint appendix makes Zare or Zerah the father of Jobab-Job.

Zebulun.note: Zebulun is Joseph's paternal half-brother; no individual encounter is narrated.

Zophar the Naamathite.note: Zophar debates Job and claims that Job deserves still greater punishment.

Zophar the Naamathite.myth: Job intercedes for the rebuked friends
Zophar the Naamathite.note: Job’s prayer accompanies Zophar’s required closing sacrifice.

Zulaykhā/Rāʿīl.note: Later Islamic literature names the master's wife and expands her pursuit of Joseph.
Persian romance makes the restored, repentant Zulaykhā Joseph's lawful wife.

the Gnostic creator/ruler.note: A subordinate cosmic ruler creates or divides Adam and Eve, who formerly possessed superior glory.

the Son of Man.myth: Three days in fish and earth
the Son of Man.note: Matthew compares Jonah’s three days in the fish with the Son of Man’s burial.

the accuser.myth: The heavenly challenge and two tests
the accuser.note: The accuser challenges Job’s piety and inflicts losses, bereavement, and disease.

the angels.note: The angels fail Adam’s naming test and prostrate before him at God’s command.
Ministering angels debate whether Adam or humanity should be created.

the devil.note: Medieval Christian allegory casts Sisera as the devil and Jael as his vanquisher.

the elder daughter.note: Lot is the father of the elder daughter.
She intoxicates Lot and has intercourse with him while he is unaware.

the serpent.note: The serpent disputes God’s warning and deceives Eve into eating.

the two angels.note: The angels seize Lot and his family, lead them out and protect him.
Lot shelters the disguised angels and prepares them a feast.

the younger daughter.note: Lot is the father of the younger daughter.
She has intercourse with the intoxicated Lot while he is unaware.

Ṣakhr.note: In later Islamic accounts, Ṣakhr steals Solomon's ring or occupies his throne.
